name: Hassan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior feeder operator at a large mine. I watch rock go into the crusher, check the belt and stop the line when a jam needs clearing. I use an AI tool most days to quiz myself on fault codes, then check the real manual with a senior operator. I like solving the puzzle, but the lower wage and uncertain shifts keep us close to the next bill.

say: I use **AI fault quizzes** to learn, but I still check the feeder and manual.
I want **safety sign-off** left with a trained person.
think: I like a **slow change** while I learn the feeder at 58.
I have **half a month** saved, so cancelled shifts still worry me.
do: **Check** AI fault-code explanations against the manual with a senior operator.
**Save** one overtime hour of pay whenever offered after bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about pay despite comfort with a small AI tool.
S0.quote: I have caught an AI answer that matched a different feeder model.
fieldNote: **Daily AI use** helps a late-entry junior study fault codes, while a senior operator verifies the answers.
**Half-month cushion** and low pay make ordinary roster changes more important than mild AI.

steps.text: Keep working assigned junior feeder shifts
Check AI fault explanations against the machine manual
Save one overtime hour of pay if offered after bills are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crusher crew I already use an AI tool to quiz myself on fault codes, but it does not clear a jam or sign a safety check. A mild future would let me keep learning the feeder without a new crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like the tool because I am new to this machine at 58. The hard part is money: my partner and I have about half a month of expenses saved. My junior rate is low, and a cancelled shift means deciding which bill can wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my feeder shifts and make a short fault-code card from the manual, checking every AI explanation with the experienced operator. In the first year I would put the pay from one extra hour into savings whenever overtime is offered and household bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, though I am calm about the software. I could live with a slow tool year if the roster stays steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets paid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We pay rent and food before the phone plan. I need the phone for the shift messages, so I would ask for a cheaper plan before I cut it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks your card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My coworker Lina, the senior feeder operator, checks the fault numbers against the actual manual. I have caught an AI answer that matched a different feeder model.

say: I expect **orders and shift sheets** to change before the crusher floor.
I would try a **tested fault display** and record wrong alerts.
think: I worry about **office posts** shrinking first.
I cannot assume **full junior hours** if slower robots reach the feeder later.
do: **Observe** the approved fault display with maintenance supervision.
**Log** false alerts during paid shifts in the first year.
**Ask** about paid control training if a robot trial is announced.
feel: **Anxious** about future hours despite interest in the technical work.
S1.quote: I enjoy the technical puzzle, but enjoyment is not the same as steady wages.
fieldNote: **Testing discipline** is concrete: false sensor alerts get recorded and verified by maintenance.
**Training interest** is only an enquiry here; no course place or paid offer exists.
**Office losses** register with him as a warning, not a reason to celebrate his own temporary safety.

steps.text: Test the approved fault display under maintenance supervision
Log false alerts during paid feeder shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning software will change orders and shift sheets before it changes the crusher floor. I would try a new fault display after the maintenance team has tested it, and I would report wrong alerts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose posts first, and I do not wish that on anyone. Slower robots could reach the feeder later; as a junior worker, I cannot assume I would keep full hours. I am willing to learn a proven display, but unpaid hours would make that impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance lead for a supervised demonstration when the display is approved. In the first year I would log false alerts during my paid shifts and ask about the mine’s paid control training if a robot trial is announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I enjoy the technical puzzle, but enjoyment is not the same as steady wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a false alert look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A screen might call a belt jam when the sensor is dirty. I would note the time, clean the sensor under the normal safety procedure and let maintenance verify the fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the office staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner that planners could face cuts before the crusher crew. We would keep our spending tight because another family’s loss can be a warning about ours.

say: I distinguish **2028 shift plans** from capable feeder robots around 2031.
I want **jam-clearing workers** involved before the mine cuts a roster.
think: I expect **most junior shifts** to disappear if capable feeder robots work.
I have **half a month** saved and few nearby openings if my hours collapse.
do: **Check** requirements for a paid process-control certificate now.
**Enrol** after 2028 if the mine funds a place and keeps my shifts.
**Apply** for advertised control work, or local plant work if none appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major shift losses and sleepless roster checking.
S2.quote: I keep waking up and opening the roster app to count shifts that have not even been assigned yet.
fieldNote: **Late junior role** and a half-month cushion explain why a 2031 robot roster feels urgent.
**Course funding and wages** are explicit conditions before he would enrol.
**Local plant work** is a fallback only if no control post is advertised.

steps.text: Enrol in process-control training if the mine funds it and shifts continue
Apply for advertised control-room work if a post opens
Apply for local plant work if no control post appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew full thinking AI in 2028 could write the shift plans, while capable robots for the feeder follow around 2031. We should test the machines with the people who clear real jams before any roster is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 by the robot date. If a robot can clear jams and run the feeder, I expect many junior shifts to go, including most of mine. Our half-month cushion would be gone before I found another mine, and there are few nearby openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the training office what a paid process-control certificate requires. In the first year after 2028 I would enrol if the mine funds a place and keeps my shifts during lessons, then apply for any advertised control-room post; if no post appears, I would look for local plant work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I keep waking up and opening the roster app to count shifts that have not even been assigned yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner that 2028 changes planning first and around 2031 threatens my feeder shifts. We would price the next month of rent and food before I committed to anything unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why control work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have learned the feeder’s fault codes and I like tracking a problem. I know a control-room job would need a certificate and an actual opening, not just my interest.

say: I see **2031 planning** change before capable feeder robots around 2034.
I want **course and pension** figures while there is time to decide.
think: I might need **wages at 66** if the pension leaves a gap.
I could use a **funded certificate** if a paid place and future job exist.
do: **Request** a pension estimate and course schedule this year.
**Take** the process-control course after 2031 if funded with shifts retained.
**Save** an extra shift payment after rent is covered.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings and whether a paid course actually opens.
S3.quote: I would not spend rent money on a private certificate with no job attached.
fieldNote: **Age 66** at robot arrival makes pension adequacy a real alternative to retraining, not a certainty.
**Funded course** depends on continued shifts; he refuses a private fee taken from rent.
**Extra saving** occurs only after rent is paid.

steps.text: Take the process-control course if funded with shifts retained
Save one extra shift payment after rent is covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2031 changes the planning desk, and capable feeder robots around 2034 affect the crusher floor. Five years to the first change is enough time to check a course and the pension, if the mine shares real figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when the robots arrive. I might want to retire, but our savings are too small to call that a plan before I see a pension statement. A funded control certificate could give me options if I still need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request a pension estimate and the process-control course schedule. In the first year after 2031 I would take the course if the mine pays and lets me keep my shifts, and put any extra paid shift into emergency savings after rent is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to plan. More time matters if the paid course exists and I can build something beyond half a month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course never opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the maintenance lead about paid practice with the approved display, if that job remains. I would not spend rent money on a private certificate with no job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide on retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would put pension income beside rent, food and medicines. If the pension leaves a gap, I would keep seeking paid shifts.

say: I see **2036 planning** change before feeder robots around 2039.
I want **safe training** and clear pension figures during the long warning.
think: I hope to leave **full feeder shifts** before age 71.
I may still need **part-time wages** if pension income cannot cover rent.
do: **Keep** current feeder shifts and review pension estimates yearly.
**Seek** public pension advice after 2036 with rent figures.
**Apply** for a local part-time plant job if the pension leaves a gap.
feel: **Anxious** about later income despite more time to prepare.
S4.quote: I hope I am not working full feeder shifts at 71, but half a month of savings does not make retirement real.
fieldNote: **Age 68** at thinking AI and 71 at robots directs attention to pension income first.
**Bus-accessible weighbridge** is a concrete possible fallback, not an assumed vacancy.
**Adult children** are conversation partners rather than a planned income source.

steps.text: Keep current feeder shifts and review pension estimates yearly
Seek public pension advice after 2036 with rent figures
Apply for local part-time plant work if pension income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches the planning desk in 2036 and capable feeder robots arrive around 2039. A decade gives us time to train safely and show workers what their pension will cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 at the robot date. I hope I am not working full feeder shifts at 71, but half a month of savings does not make retirement real. I might need a small paid role if the pension falls short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts, use the approved fault display only after maintenance verifies it and review the pension estimate each year with my partner. In the first year after 2036 I would ask a public adviser to check pension against rent, then apply for a local part-time plant job if there is a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement money, even with a distant robot date. The extra years give me more chances to prepare, but I need actual income at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What local job would fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the materials yard about a part-time weighbridge opening, since I can read load sheets and reach the yard by bus. I would check the pay before leaving any feeder shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk with them, but I would not put their income into our budget. They have their own work and homes to manage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect capable feeder robots around 2031 to take most junior shifts. A funded process-control certificate with paid time and an actual job opening would help. We also need clear staffing numbers before the mine replaces people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the training hours. A course I can only attend after an unpaid shift is not a route to a new wage.

headlineQuote: A course I can only attend after an unpaid shift is not a route to a new wage.
portrait: **Hassan, 58**, operates a crusher feeder and checks his daily AI fault-code study with a senior worker.
**Half a month** of savings and lower pay make cancelled shifts a household worry even if AI barely changes.
**Early tool use** suits him, but he insists on safe tests, paid training and a real control job.
**Fast AGI** alarms him because 2028 planning change could lead to capable feeder robots and lost junior shifts around 2031.
**Longer warning** allows pension checks and conditional control training, while retirement income remains uncertain at 66 or 71.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could lead to major junior feeder-shift losses around 2031 before he can afford retirement.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded process-control training** with paid time and an advertised job would give him a viable route.
**Clear staffing numbers** would let the crew plan before a robot trial removes shifts.
